tagline: Across the Uwharrie foothills, a river crossing and a gold discovery
intro: NC 49 skirts the northern foothills of the Uwharrie Mountains and crosses the Yadkin River near Tuckertown Reservoir. Northeast of Mount Pleasant, it becomes a designated North Carolina Scenic Byway. NCDOT describes its byway program as a way to experience the state’s history, geography and culture.

The highway number came first to a shorter road: NC 49 was established in late 1934 between Lake Wylie and Charlotte. In 1940, an extension carried the number northeast to Virginia, replacing NC 62 through Richfield and Farmer to Asheboro. In 1953, a new routing bypassed Concord.

Traveling northeast, start with Mount Pleasant, whose town center lies south of NC 49. Richfield marks the junction with US 52. Beyond the river crossing, the highway skirts the foothills before descending into the Asheboro area.

moments.title: Reed Gold Mine
moments.text: In 1799, Conrad Reed found a 17-pound yellow rock in Little Meadow Creek on his family’s farm. It served as a doorstop for three years before a Fayetteville jeweler identified it as gold in 1802. John Reed asked $3.50 for it, the equivalent of a week’s wages. Mining later moved underground in 1831; the last underground work at Reed Mine took place in 1912. The mine in Midland is a National Historic Landmark, recognized for the first documented commercial gold find in the United States. The nugget’s true value was around $3,600.

moments.title: Tuckertown crossing
moments.text: The NC 49 bridge crosses Tuckertown Reservoir, where the Yadkin occupies a narrow valley at the western edge of the Uwharrie Mountains. The reservoir lies between High Rock Dam and Tuckertown Dam. Its water serves hydroelectric power generation. Alcoa historically operated the lake’s power generation before selling it to Cube Hydro Carolinas in February 2017.

moments.title: Denton
moments.text: Denton’s railroad story began with a strip of land. In 1906, Branson Ivey Harrison sold a right-of-way for the Thomasville and Glen Anna Railroad to reach the town. Regular service began in 1912, after the line became the Carolina and Yadkin Railroad and extended to High Rock. Timber drove the resulting growth: during the peak years of 1917–1918, Denton shipped nearly 200,000 railroad cross ties annually. The town had previously been Finch’s Cross Roads; its Denton post office opened in 1878 with Samuel Moses Peacock as postmaster. Peacock had suggested the name after a town in Texas.
